title: Trump officials scramble to manage fallout after his $5K check pledge to all Americans | CNN Politics
text:
President Donald Trump blindsided many of his own administration officials and allies with his vow to pay all American adults $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress, prompting an internal scramble on Thursday to backfill the proposal’s specifics, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.

Trump made the pledge during his speech at the GOP’s midterm convention after discussing it with only a small circle of close political advisers, including Jason Miller and James Blair, a Trump political adviser told CNN. That left most officials across the administration unprepared to manage the fallout of a $1 trillion proposal that has already faced widespread blowback over its price tag and feasibility.

Several Republican lawmakers immediately panned the idea as a misguided ploy ahead of November’s midterm elections that would be nearly impossible to pass through Congress — not to mention one that would violate many of the party’s core economic principles. Even on the convention floor, some attendees were skeptical.

“I’m not into free stuff,” Arlington small business owner Wilma May told CNN in Dallas. “I would prefer him to give $5,000 towards paying down the deficit.”

The vow also alarmed GOP economists and some close Trump allies, some of whom dismissed it as a poor attempt to effectively bribe voters to keep Republicans in power.

“It’s a mystery that everybody’s trying to get to the bottom of, whose idea this was,” said Stephen Moore, an outside economic adviser to Trump, who opposes the idea. “The problem with sending people checks is it actually has a negative economic consequence.”

Trump offered few details about the proposal during his speech on Wednesday night, suggesting only that it might draw on revenue collected as a result of tariffs on foreign goods. Trump has previously floated a series of other “dividends” for all Americans funded by tariff revenue or other savings, but has yet to deliver on them.

On Thursday, White House officials spent the morning racing to sort out the logistics required to make good on this latest unprecedented promise, one official said.

But a subsequent fact sheet released by the White House indicated that those efforts remained a work in progress; it provided no details on how the government envisioned funding the payments or where the money would come from.

“The same leadership that shattered the old limits of what Washington thought possible is now prepared to put $5,000 directly into Americans’ pockets,” the White House said, without providing specifics.

A White House official disputed the notion that Trump had caught his aides off guard, telling CNN that he had “discussed this idea with his senior staff in the lead up to the speech. There was no surprise.”

In a statement, White House spokesman Davis Ingle did not directly address the prospect of paying all American adults $5,000 if Republicans keep the House and Senate.

“The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump,” he said. “With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results.”

Trump’s surprise pledge comes as he struggles to combat rising voter frustration over the cost of living and his economic policies. For months, polling has shown Americans deeply dissatisfied with the president’s handling of inflation.

The ongoing war with Iran has only worsened the broader economic environment facing Republicans, sending gas and diesel prices soaring once again in recent weeks, with no clear end in sight. As the GOP gathered in Dallas this week, both the global and US benchmark prices for oil rose above the $100-per-barrel mark, and diesel hit a record $5.98 a gallon, on average, on Thursday.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed the affordability concerns, dismissing the term on Wednesday night as an issue ginned up by Democrats to damage him politically and insisting that that US is in the midst of a “the most successful two years financially and every other way.”

Yet in a tacit acknowledgment that economic woes are weighing on the GOP, the administration in recent weeks has increasingly sought to highlight steps aimed at lowering some everyday costs, like the price of ground beef and certain medicines.

Trump, who signed off on sending Americans two rounds of $1,200 stimulus checks during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, has repeatedly returned to the idea of sending cash directly to voters as a way to win political support.

Last year, he floated the prospect of $5,000 “DOGE dividends” tied to the supposed savings created by his slashing of the federal workforce. More recently, Trump vowed to send out $2,000 checks funded by tariff revenue. Neither have happened.

Trump’s latest proposal faces even longer odds — a reality that prompted many skeptics, including some Trump allies, to dismiss the idea as a purely political maneuver.

“For the record, I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this admin, but am strongly against bread and circus bribes,” Joe Lonsdale, a GOP donor close to Donald Trump Jr., wrote Wednesday night on X. Lonsdale co-hosted a major fundraiser on the sidelines of the convention Wednesday night with Trump Jr. and other high-profile Republicans, sources familiar with the event said.

Congressional Republicans would need to write and pass legislation authorizing the more than $1 trillion in payments – a sum that would equal more than half of the amount the government spent on all discretionary spending in the 2025 fiscal year, according to the Congressional Budget Office. And while some lawmakers immediately backed the idea — Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio pledged to have a bill ready by November — the proposal surprised GOP leadership, who had not had any prior discussions about it, a person familiar with the matter said.

In a Fox News interview airing Thursday, Trump seemed to acknowledge that Congress would need to approve the proposal, blaming Democrats for standing in the way of his ability to follow through on the pledge sooner. But he then contradicted himself, saying in a CBS interview that while Republicans “will do it if we needed it,” he believed he could deliver the payments without congressional action.

The idea also hinges on the president’s party keeping control of the House and Senate — a midterm outcome that would defy polling trends and decades of political precedent.

“The danger he has is that the way it was rolled out, it will sound like a gimmick,” said former House GOP Speaker Newt Gingrich, who added that he’s previously talked to Trump about distributing money generated by tariffs, but was surprised Wednesday night’s announcement.

There are also myriad economic concerns that likely make such a proposal unlikely to become anything more than a political talking point. Trump’s proposal would blow a $1.2 trillion hole in the federal budget, which is already contending with a swiftly-rising debt level, according to at least two estimates.

Tariffs wouldn’t come close to covering the tab. New tariffs in 2027 would only raise enough revenue to pay for about one-tenth of the cost, according to the Tax Foundation, a right-leaning think tank.

“A deficit-financed dividend payment of this scale would signal to markets that the US is not serious about getting its fiscal house in order,” Erica York, a senior economist at the foundation, said in a statement. “It would risk further rises in interest rates, add to inflationary pressures, and worsen the very problems that are trying to be ‘solved’ by the proposal.”

Another federal budget watchdog group called the idea “fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious.”

“This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation, and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy,” Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement.

Trump’s proposal comes as the United States is digging itself into an ever-deeper debt hole. The federal debt hit a record $40 trillion in mid-August, an inauspicious milestone that will have consequences for Americans, businesses and the government for years to come.

Even without the dividend checks, the federal government is forecast to run a budget deficit of nearly $1.9 trillion in fiscal year 2027, which starts October 1.

“It’s not an economic growth proposal,” said Moore, adding even if Republicans had the money to spend, it’d be better invested elsewhere. “With that amount of money you could cut the payroll tax by one or two percentage points, you could cut income tax by two to three points. That would actually provide an economic incentive.”

CNN’s Steve Contorno contributed to this report.
